An ending is added to the end of a word. After a p, k, s, sh or ch sound, the ending e d says t. Jumped, packed, wished.
After a b, g, m, n or l sound, the ending e d says d. Hugged, filled, planned, grinned.
After a t or a d, the ending e d adds a whole new part that says ed. Hunt-ed. Land-ed. Listen for two parts.
The ending s says s after a p, t or k sound, as in cats. After most other sounds it says z, as in dogs.

T and h say th. Put your tongue between your teeth and push the air out.

If the part before ends in a vowel, it says its name: ta-ble. If it ends in a consonant, the vowel is short: can-dle.
Remember: count back three letters from the end. Consonant plus l e is the last part.
Some words can be split two ways. Cabin can be ca-bin or cab-in. Try one way, then try the other.
Try the open split first, so the vowel says its name. If it does not sound like a word you know, flip to the closed split, so the vowel is short.
A part you say softly may sound like uh. Wag-on. Lem-on. Pet-al. Listen for the quiet part.
Remember: if a split does not sound like a word, flip it. Open says its name, closed is short. A quiet part may say uh.
An open syllable ends in a vowel. Nothing closes the door, so the vowel says its name. Be, he, me, we.
The o says its name too: go, no, so.
The i says its name in hi. Pro and fro are open too.
Compare a closed word and an open word. Closed has a short vowel. Open says its name.
Remember: if a syllable ends in a vowel, the door is open and the vowel says its name.
One consonant sits between two vowels. Try splitting before the consonant: ro-bot.
The first part ends in a vowel, so its door is open and the vowel says its name: ro, mu, ho.
The second part ends in a consonant, so its vowel is short: bot, sic, tel.
Remember: one consonant between two vowels, split before it. The first part is open and says its name. The second part is closed and is short.
At the end of a longer word, the letter y says long e. Ba-by. Hap-py. Fun-ny.
At the end of a short word, the letter y says long i. My. Fly. Try. Sky.
In a longer word, the y makes a part of its own. Ba-by. Ti-ny. Na-vy.
Remember: at the end of a short word, y says long i. At the end of a longer word, y says long e.
An r syllable has a vowel followed by r. The r changes the vowel sound, so it is not short and it is not long.
Ar says ar, as in car. Open your mouth wide.
Or says or, as in fork. Round your lips.
In long words, the vowel and the r stay together when you divide. Gar-den. Tar-get. For-est.
Remember: a vowel followed by r makes a new sound. A r says ar and o r says or.
E r, i r and u r all say the same sound. Fern. Bird. Turn.
There are three spellings for one sound. You cannot hear which one it is, so look at the letters. First. Shirt. Third. Hurt. Surf. Burst.
E r is the most common spelling at the end of a word. After. Sister. Winter. Number.
Remember: e r, i r and u r all say the same sound. A word ending in the sound usually uses the letters e r.
Long words can have an r part and other parts. Divide first, then name each part. Car-pen-ter.
Keep each vowel and r together. Do not split them. Gar-den-ing. Mar-ket-ing. Re-port-ing.
The last part is often quiet. Car-pen-ter. Yes-ter-day. Say it softly.
Remember: divide a long word, keep each vowel and r together, and say the last part softly.
A vowel team syllable has two vowel letters working together as a team to say one sound. In rain, a and i together say long a.
A i goes in the middle of a word. A y goes at the end. Both say long a.
When you divide a long word, the team stays together. Rail-way. Ex-plain. Dis-play.
Remember: a i in the middle and a y at the end are a team. They say long a.
A u and a w both say aw. A u sits inside a word, and a w ends a word. Sauce. Haul. Saw. Draw.
O i and o y both say oy. O i sits inside a word, and o y ends a word. Coin. Oil. Boy. Toy.
A w and o y often end a part in a long word. Aw-ful. En-joy. An-noy.
Remember: a u and a w say aw. O i and o y say oy. The letters inside a word are u and i. The letters at the end are w and y.
Ee says long e: tree, feet, green.
E a often says long e too. Sea. Team. Leaf. Beach.
Two spellings can make the same sound. Look at the spelling to know the word. See and sea. Meet and meat. Week and weak.
Remember: e e and e a are teams. They often say long e.
E a can also say short short e. Head. Bread. Breath. Thread.
P h says f. Phone. Photo. Graph. Dolphin.
Sometimes two vowels side by side are not a team. They belong to different parts. Li-on. Gi-ant. Du-et.
Try the team sound first. If it does not sound like a word you know, try the other sound, or split between the two vowels.
Remember: e a can say long e or short e. P h says f. Two vowels may split into two parts.
O a says long o. So does o e at the end of a word. Boat. Coat. Toe.
The letters i g h say long i. The g and the h are silent. Light. Right. High. Bright.
I e at the end of a word says long i. Pie. Tie. Lie.
Remember: o a and o e say long o. I g h and i e say long i.
The teams o o, e w and u e can say oo, as in moon. Moon. Blew. Blue.
O o can also say the short sound you hear in book. Book. Look. Good. Foot.
Try one sound. If it does not sound like a word you know, try the other sound. Room. Cook. Boot. Took.
Remember: o o has two sounds, oo as in moon and a short sound as in book. Try one, then the other.
O u says ow, as in out. Cloud. House. Mouth. Found.
O w can say ow too. Cow. Down. Town. Brown. Owl.
O w can also say long o. Snow. Grow. Slow. Yellow.
Ow has two sounds. Try ow first. If it does not sound like a word you know, flip to long o. Cow and crow. Brown and blown.
Remember: o u says ow. O w has two sounds, ow and long o. Try one, and flip if it is not a word.
That is the pattern. Now you know how it works.
A new pattern to discover, apprentice. Look closely at what comes next.
Now you try. Read this word out loud.
A long word can have three parts. Divide two times. Cel-e-brate.
Look for the silent e part at the end of the word, then work backward. Nav-i-gate.
Say the middle part softly. The loud parts are the first and the last. Dom-i-nate. Ded-i-cate.
Remember: divide a long word into parts, find the silent e part at the end, and say the middle part softly.
A silent e syllable has a vowel, a consonant, then an e at the end. The e is silent, and it makes the vowel say its name.
The letters a, consonant, e say long a, as in cake. The letters e, consonant, e say long e, as in these.
i-e says long i: bike, five, line, smile.
o-e says long o: home, bone, note, stone.
The letters u, consonant, e say long u, as in cube and cute. They can also say oo, as in rule and flute.
Remember: vowel, consonant, silent e. The e is silent, and the vowel says its name.
The letter c before e, i or y says s. Cell. City. Nice. We call it soft c.
The letter g before e, i or y can say j. Gem. Page. Huge. We call it soft g.
At the end of a word, c e and g e keep a silent e. It keeps the c soft and the g soft. Dance. Fence. Change.
Before a, o or u, c says k and g says g. Cat. Cup. Gap. Gum.
Remember: c before e, i or y says s, and g before e, i or y can say j. Before a, o or u they stay hard.
A silent e syllable can be the end of a long word. In-vite. Un-safe. Ex-cuse. The same rule: the vowel says its name.
Divide the word first. Then look for the silent e at the end of the last part. Com-pete. Con-fuse. Ex-plode.
In the letters k n, the k is silent. Knife. Knot. In w r, the w is silent. Write. Wrap.
Remember: a silent e part can finish a long word. In kn the k is silent, and in wr the w is silent.
Syllable Quest is for readers who need more practice with long words.

You looked at the vowel and at what comes after it. That decides the type.
Right clan. The ending of the part told you.
You sorted it by how the vowel is held. That is the skill.
Yes. You looked at the whole letter group, not just one letter.
Two letters, one sound. You spotted it.
That sound matches its letters. Your eyes and ears agree.
You used the patterns you know to read that long word.

Every part is in its place. That is how long words get written.

Listen to the sound. Then write a spelling for it in your Word Book.
Look at the mouth picture. See where the lips and tongue go, then say it that way.
Look at the letters on the card. Say the sound they make.
Sound Check, apprentice. Let's warm up the sounds we know.
Two small words can hold hands to make one bigger word, like a bridge over a gully.
Read each small word, then join them, and the bridge holds firm.
A gust of wind pushes a page onto the trail, with a tiny ending stuck to it.
Endings like -s, -es and -ed can stick to a word, like tags on a backpack.
The first torn page hides behind a rock, and short words will free it.
Read each short word one sound at a time, and the path opens up.
The last cliff holds a long word, but it is only three small closed pieces stacked together.
Split it into three parts, read each part, and then put the parts back together.
Three consonants in the middle can look tricky, but keep a blend together, and otherwise split after the second consonant.
A hundred stone steps climb the cliff, and you can read every one of them.
When two matching letters sit in the middle, the word splits between them.
A rabbit guards the trail, and its name has two matching letters in the middle.
Two different consonants stand in the middle, and the word breaks between them.
A camp cook dropped a napkin on the trail, and the split between nap and kin shows the way.
The first pages of the Great Word Book glow, and the canyon walls are steady again.
The Keeper smiles and says, 'Closed Canyon is clear. Next, the islands where open sounds sing.'
The first torn page landed in Closed Canyon, where every short vowel is shut in tight.
A consonant closes the door after a short vowel, like a latch on a gate.
Follow the wind into the canyon, and let's see what the walls can teach you.
A storm tore through the library, and the Great Word Book flew off its shelf.
Its pages blew across the land, and the words on them went quiet.
The Keeper of Words said, 'I need an apprentice to read these words back into place. Will you help?'
All six crests now shine, and every torn page of the Great Word Book is back on its shelf.
The Keeper hands you the Great Word Book and says, 'You read every land. Well done, apprentice.'
Far across the water, the City of Builders waits, and it is coming later.
The lake sparkles, and the Great Word Book is nearly whole again.
The Keeper says, 'Well done. Every land has its words back, and one more story is waiting.'
Little Tail Lake sits at the far end of the map, and its words end in a special pattern.
A consonant followed by le often finishes a word, and it makes a soft last syllable.
Find the last pages here, and listen for the sound that le makes at the end.
A little fish swims past, and its name has twin letters just before the final le.
Split the word before the twin letters, then read the last part as consonant and le.
The last path around the lake holds a candle, a puzzle and many other long words.
Take each part one at a time, use every pattern you learned, and the lake path is complete.
A table sits by the lake, and its name ends with a consonant and le.
The consonant and le make the last syllable, so say the ending sound clearly.
The Open Sky Isles are bright again, and the pages ride the wind like kites.
The Keeper says, 'The next forest hides silent e's, and they change the vowels around them.'
Open Sky Isles float above the clouds, and many of their words end in a long, open vowel.
Here a vowel is free to say its own name, with no consonant door to shut it in.
The next torn pages drifted up here, so climb the rope bridges and follow them.
A cabin floats in the clouds, but the first split does not match the sound.
Flip the split to the other side, try again, and the word will click into place.
The first island has a single vowel at the end of a word, and that vowel says its name.
Words like she and go open wide, so the vowel is the first sound you hear.
A robot clanks into a local hotel, and its name splits right after the open first vowel.
When a vowel stands alone at the end of the first part, it often says its own name, so read it long.
A baby bunny hops by a cloud, and its name ends with a y that sings a long e.
At the end of a word, y can take the long e sound, so listen for the bunny's name.
The mountains are quiet, and the bossy r pages shine in the Great Word Book.
The Keeper says, 'Little Tail Lake is next, where a little l and a silent e hide at the ends of words.'
Bossy-R Mountains are tall and rocky, and the r there is very bossy.
An r right after a vowel takes charge and changes the sound that vowel makes.
Climb the mountain path, find the torn pages, and listen to what the bossy r tells the vowel to do.
A garden grows on the mountainside, and ar in its name makes a sound all its own.
Or works the same way, so a fork at the picnic table teaches the bossy r sound.
A bird sits on a perch, and its name has er, ir and ur, which sound alike.
Er, ir and ur all make the same sound, so the bird's song hides three spellings for one note.
A carpenter builds a shelter on the mountain, and the tool list has ar, or, er, ir and ur.
Read each bossy r word one part at a time, and the mountain shelter stands tall.
The harbor boats are sailing again, and the team pages are back in the Great Word Book.
The Keeper says, 'Next are the mountains, where an r changes the vowel right before it.'
Vowel Team Harbor is busy with boats, and its vowels travel in pairs.
Two vowels side by side can work as a team, and together they make one new sound.
Find the torn pages on the docks, and listen for the sound each team makes.
A lady waves from the bay, and the words on her sail hold ai and ay.
When ai or ay appears, the pair says the long a sound, so read the pair together.
A hawk circles the boat, and the aw in its name makes a bold sound.
Oi and oy share one sound, like a coin dropping onto the deck.
Seaweed floats near the pier, and its name holds a pair of vowels that say long e.
Ee and ea often say the long e sound, so read the pair as one clear note.
A harbor breakfast table holds many team words, and each pair has its own sound.
Read each pair of vowels carefully, check which sound fits, and the whole table comes alive.
A raincoat hangs on the pier, and its name holds oa, which says long o.
Igh and ie both say the long i sound, like a kite flying high over the harbor.
A balloon floats over the harbor, and its name has two o's that sing the long oo sound.
Ew and ue can say the oo sound too, so try one sound, then listen and try again.
A brown owl sits on a rainbow over the harbor, and both brown and owl use ow.
Ou and ow can say the ow sound in a cloud, or the long o sound in a bowl.
The silent e's stayed quiet, but they did the work, and the forest pages are back.
The Keeper nods and says, 'Vowel Team Harbor is next, where two vowels work together.'
Silent-E Forest is thick with tall trees, and many of its words end with a quiet e.
That e makes no sound itself, but it tells the vowel before it to say its own name.
Find the torn pages in the forest, and listen for the vowels that say their names.
The deepest part of the forest hides a long word with three parts and several silent e's.
Read each part with its vowel, check each silent e, and the whole path opens up.
A cake sits on a log, and the silent e at its end tells the a to say its name.
Hear the long vowel, let the e stay quiet, and the page slides out of the bramble.
A page by the lake has a soft c and a soft g, and their sounds change before e or i.
Hear c go soft like s, and g go soft like j, and the words open up for you.
A long word in the forest has two parts, and the silent e helps you find the split.
Say the first part with its long vowel, then the second part, and join them smoothly.
I will read a sentence, and then you read it back to me.
A mistake means a pattern we haven't practiced enough yet. This page will be ready next time.
The page is whole again, apprentice. You read it with care. Well done.

Stand up and hold one arm out in front of you.
Tap down your arm, one tap for each letter, and say each letter as you tap.
Now slide your hand down your arm and say the whole word.
Say the word once more. Think about the tricky part.
